teaser: A bronze figure with no arms and no face, built to show speed itself.

lesson.text: How would you make a statue of speed? Not of a runner, frozen at one instant like a photograph, but of the running: the push, the rush of air, the place the body was half a second ago. In 1913 a 30-year-old Italian named Umberto Boccioni gave himself exactly that problem.

Boccioni belonged to the Futurists, a group of young Italian artists and poets in love with everything fast and new: trains, engines, electric light, crowds. They found their country's museums suffocating. He was a painter first, and had been making sculpture for only about a year.

Futurism was launched in 1909 on the front page of a Paris newspaper. Its manifesto, a public declaration of aims, claimed that a roaring racing car was more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace, the ancient Greek winged statue in the Louvre.

His idea: a moving body does not stop at its skin. It drags air behind it, and our eye smears one position into the next. So he modeled both at once, the muscle and its wake, as a single solid. That is the “continuity in space” of the title. The figure stands just over a meter tall (about 44 inches).

lesson.title: A body at full stride
lesson.text: From this angle the figure walks toward the left. Go from head to feet.

spots.title: The head
spots.text: No eyes, no mouth. The face is a sharp ridge crossed by another, somewhere between a helmet and a machine part. This is nobody in particular.

spots.title: No arms
spots.text: The chest swells forward like a hull cutting water, and the shoulders simply end. Boccioni drops the arms so nothing interrupts the forward drive.

spots.title: The trailing leg
spots.text: Behind the calf, bronze streams out in pointed lobes like flames or a flag in wind. It is the air the leg has just pushed through, made solid.

spots.title: Two blocks
spots.text: Each foot is planted on its own small block instead of one shared base. The gap between them makes the stride feel longer, like a step across a ditch.

lesson.text: Now the funny part. A striding figure, no arms, drapery flying backward: that describes the Victory of Samothrace almost word for word. The Futurists wanted to burn the past down, and Boccioni's most famous work rhymes with the very statue their manifesto mocked.
Boccioni's leap was to sculpt what a body does to the space around it. The shapes that look like armor or flames are motion, given a form you can walk around.

He modeled the figure in plaster, cheap and white, and that is all he ever saw. In 1915 Italy entered the First World War and Boccioni, who had cheered for it, enlisted. In August 1916 he was thrown from his horse during cavalry training and died the next day. He was 33.

Every bronze version of this sculpture, including the one in this photo, was cast after the artist's death, the first in 1931. Boccioni had written against bronze and marble as tired “noble” materials, so the gleaming gold surface was not his choice.

He had made several other striding figures in plaster that same year. After his death they were broken up and lost. This is the only one that survived, and its original plaster ended up far from Italy, in a museum in São Paulo, Brazil.
Millions of Europeans carry this sculpture around without knowing it. Italy chose it for the back of its 20-cent euro coin.
Go back to the opening question. The answer weighs many kilos of metal and has stood still on a pedestal for over a century, and it still looks as if it is about to leave the room.

quiz.question: What did the Futurists admire most?
quiz.explanation: They loved trains, engines and crowds, and found museums suffocating.

quiz.question: What are the flame-like shapes behind the legs?
options: The moving air and motion, made solid
quiz.explanation: Boccioni modeled the body and its wake as one continuous form.

quiz.question: Which material did Boccioni himself use for this figure?
quiz.explanation: He only ever saw it in plaster; the bronzes were cast after he died.

quiz.question: Which ancient statue does the figure oddly resemble?
quiz.explanation: Like the Victory, it strides forward without arms, with forms flying backward.

quiz.question: How did Boccioni die?
options: After falling from a horse during army training
quiz.explanation: He was thrown from his horse in 1916, aged 33.

facts.text: Boccioni supervised the casting of the bronze himself.
facts.explanation: All bronze casts were made after his death in 1916, the first in 1931.

facts.text: The sculpture appears on an Italian euro coin.
facts.explanation: It is on the back of Italy's 20-cent coin.

facts.text: The figure's face has carefully detailed eyes and a mouth.
facts.explanation: The head has no features, only crossing ridges like a helmet.
